tip: No 'I' needed – the -ω ending of πίνω (pino) already marks the speaker. Greek drops subject pronouns unless you're stressing who does it.
Greek questions keep statement word order – no 'do'. Εσύ τρως κρέας; (esi tros kreas) = 'you eat meat?', asked by tone alone. That ; at the end is the Greek question mark.
Negation is just δεν (den) before the verb: δεν τρώω (den troo) = 'I don't eat'. No helper word like English 'do'.
Thirst is a verb in Greek: διψάει (dipsai) means 'is thirsty' – the baby thirsts. Hunger works the same way: πεινάει (peinai).
Talking about cheese in general still needs 'the': το τυρί (to tiri). Greek keeps the article where English drops it.
'The bill' changes shape as an object: ο λογαριασμός (o logariasmos) becomes τον λογαριασμό (ton logariasmo). Articles and endings shift with the noun's role.
'One' matches its noun: ένα τσάι (ena tsai) but έναν καφέ (enan kafe) – masculine nouns as objects add -ν to the word for 'one'.
One word covers to, in, and at: σε (se). It fuses with 'the': σε + την becomes στην αγορά (stin agora) = to the market.
Πάμε (pame) is both 'we go' and 'let's go / shall we?' – the same form makes the statement and the invitation.
English says 'on foot'; Greek says with the feet – με τα πόδια (me ta podia), article included.
Cities take 'the': από την Αθήνα (apo tin Athina) is literally 'from the Athens'. Countries too – η Ελλάδα (i Ellada).
Clock times are 'at the...': στις εφτά (stis efta) = at seven. The 'the' is plural because hours count as plural in Greek.
One present tense does both English ones: δουλεύω (doulevo) = 'I work' and 'I am working'. Greek has no separate -ing form.
Possession keeps the article and puts 'my' after: τη μητέρα μου (ti mitera mou) = 'the mother of-me'. Μου (mou) never comes before the noun.
Time of day needs no 'in': το βράδυ (to vradi) = in the evening, literally just 'the evening'. Mornings match: το πρωί (to proi).
The future is just θα (tha) + verb: θα πάω (tha pao) = I will go. Θα never changes – one little word for every person and verb.
Liking flips in Greek: μου αρέσει πολύ το τυρί (mou aresi poli to tiri) = 'the cheese pleases me a lot'. You're the receiver, not the doer.
Greek has no infinitive – after να (na) the verb still conjugates: μου αρέσει να διαβάζω (mou aresi na diavazo) = 'I like that I read'.
